div.head: About the eLiebermann Project
div.p: eLiebermann is a digital research resource for the laws and legal language of early England. Its foundation is Felix Liebermann’s Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen (1903–16), still the standard complete edition of the early English laws, which it makes searchable, interlinked and accessible to readers of English. Around that core it gathers later editions, translations and scholarship, so that the text of a law, the words it uses, and what scholars have said about both can be studied in one place.
It has three parts:

list.item: The eLiebermann Guide to the Gesetze expands and translates the apparatus of the Gesetze: Liebermann’s sigla for the law codes; his list of manuscripts; his grammatical terms and abbreviations; the authors and works he cites; his own account of how to read the dictionary; and his forewords, in German and English.

div.p: The project grows out of research on the language and composition of the earliest English law codes. Its aims are to open Liebermann’s foundational work to more scholars, and to make possible new research on the earliest English written laws.
At present eLiebermann holds:

list.item: 9,090 dictionary entries, the whole of the Wörterbuch;
5,647 clauses of 124 law codes and legal texts, from the laws of Æthelberht of Kent to the Anglo-Norman law books of the twelfth century, with the ordeal rituals and excommunication formulae;
the texts and translations of later editions, among them those of F. L. Attenborough, A. J. Robertson and Dorothy Whitelock;
3,214 cross-references between clauses: 1,708 from Liebermann’s margins, notes and commentary, and the rest from later scholars.

div.p: The principles on which the texts have been edited, and the methods by which they have been transcribed, checked and encoded, are set out under Editorial Principles.

div.head: Release and corrections
div.p: eLiebermann is in public beta (version 0.9, November 2026). All of Liebermann’s laws and the whole of the Wörterbuch are on the site, but the checking of transcriptions against the printed volumes, and of links to other dictionaries, is still under way, and material is added and corrected continuously. Each dictionary entry and clause keeps a history of the changes made to it.

Corrections are welcome. Every dictionary entry and clause page has a button for suggesting a change or reporting a problem, which sends a note to the editor; reports are read and answered, and the correction is recorded in the history of the page.

div.head: Felix Liebermann and Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen
div.p: Felix Liebermann (born Berlin, 20 July 1851; died Berlin, 7 October 1925) was a German historian of medieval England, and the foremost authority of his generation on Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman law. He came from a prosperous Jewish family in Berlin; the painter Max Liebermann was his elder brother. He began in business, in banking and the textile trade, and it was while he was living in Manchester that he became interested in English history. In 1873 he went to Göttingen to study it under Georg Waitz and Reinhold Pauli, and took his doctorate in 1875 with a study of the Dialogus de Scaccario. From 1877 to 1885 he worked as an editor for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, for which he edited extracts from thirteenth-century English historians.

Liebermann held no regular university post, and spent the rest of his life as an independent scholar in Berlin. In a long series of studies he edited and explained the legal compilations of the early twelfth century through which most of the Old English laws were transmitted: the Quadripartitus (1892), the Consiliatio Cnuti (1893), the Leges Edwardi Confessoris (1896) and the Leges Henrici (1901). The universities of Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1896. His English lecture The National Assembly in the Anglo-Saxon Period appeared in 1913.
His great work, Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, was published in Halle for the Savigny-Stiftung, in three volumes and four parts:

list.item: I. Text und Übersetzung (1903): the texts of all the laws, from Æthelberht to the Anglo-Norman compilations, with the readings of every manuscript printed in parallel columns, a German translation, and marginal cross-references between clauses;
II.1. Wörterbuch (1906): a dictionary of every word in the laws;
II.2. Rechts- und Sachglossar (1912): a glossary of legal and historical subjects;
III. Einleitung zu jedem Stück; Erklärungen zu einzelnen Stellen (1916): an introduction to each text and a commentary on individual passages.

div.p: More than a century later the Gesetze remains the edition from which the laws are commonly cited, and much of what has been written on early English law since rests on it. But it is not an easy book to use. It is written in a heavily abbreviated academic German, it depends on hundreds of sigla, and its apparatus is dense and occasionally inconsistent. Parts of its scholarship have also been substantially revised by later studies. eLiebermann keeps Liebermann’s text as he printed it, and sets beside it the work of the century since.

div.head: Citing eLiebermann
div.p: Every page links to the scan of the printed page of the Gesetze on which it rests, so that the text can be checked, and cited, from the print:
Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16).
To cite eLiebermann as a whole:
Anya Adair, ed., eLiebermann: A Database of Early English Laws and Legal Language, after Felix Liebermann, version 0.9 (2026), https://anyaadair.github.io/eLiebermann/.
To cite a dictionary entry or a clause (each page gives its own citation in this form, ready to copy, under “Cite this page”):

A dictionary entry: “bocland”, in eLiebermann Legal Dictionary, ed. Anya Adair, version 0.9, https://anyaadair.github.io/eLiebermann/entry.html?id=bocland (accessed 21 November 2026); after Liebermann, Gesetze II.1, p. 26.

A clause: “Ine 23.2”, in eLiebermann Lawcodes Database, ed. Anya Adair, version 0.9, https://anyaadair.github.io/eLiebermann/law.html?id=Ine_23-2 (accessed 21 November 2026); after Liebermann, Gesetze I, p. 98.
When you quote a later edition or translation of a clause, please cite that edition too: its full reference is given on the page.

div.head: People
div.p: Anya Adair, Editor. School of English and Department of Law, The University of Hong Kong. Anya Adair directs the project, and is responsible for the creation and editing of the database and website.
Mitchell Harrop, Website and Technical Development. Mitchell Harrop designed the core of the eLiebermann website and its data infrastructure.
Allan Adair, Research Assistant and Data Entry. Allan Adair undertook a major portion of the work of keying and correcting dictionary and Old English lawcode entries against the print editions.
The project is grateful to the readers and research assistants whose corrections, sent through the site, are recorded in the histories of the entries and clauses they concern.

div.head: Use of a large language model
div.p: Parts of the work were done with the assistance of Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic: a second, independent transcription of the Wörterbuch from page images, collated word by word with the project’s own; the English renderings of Liebermann’s German and of some Latin texts, which are labelled as such on every page; and much of the encoding, linking and checking of the data. All of this work was directed and reviewed by the editor, and its details are recorded in the editorial principles and in the history of each page. Where a reading, identification or link has not yet been checked by the editor, the page says so.

div.head: Funding
div.p: The work described here was supported by a grant from the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (General Research Fund, Project No. HKU 17604022), for the project The Language and Style of the Earliest English Law Codes (PI: Anya Adair).

div.head: Rights, code and data
div.p: Liebermann’s text, translation and apparatus are in the public domain. The texts and translations of later editors are reproduced for research and teaching, with full references to the editions from which they come; they remain the copyright of their authors and publishers.

The site’s code and data are on GitHub at github.com/anyaadair/eLiebermann: the dictionary entries and clauses as TEI XML, the authority lists of law codes, manuscripts, abbreviations and works cited, the scripts that build the site, and the reports of collation and checking.
